study_identification.title: Shared differential factors underlying individual spontaneous neural activity abnormalities in major depressive disorder

study_characteristics.study_objective: To identify shared differential factors underlying individualized spontaneous neural activity (ALFF) abnormalities in major depressive disorder (MDD) by using normative modeling and non-negative matrix factorization, and to investigate how these factors relate to clinical characteristics, neurobiological substrates, and patient subtypes.

dataset_name.answer: Discovery dataset: DIDA-MDD (Disease Imaging Data Archiving-Major Depressive Disorder Working Group, 9 sites); Validation dataset: REST-meta-MDD consortium (25 sites)

hc_age.answer: Discovery dataset: mean 33.96, sd 13.87; Validation dataset: mean 36.15, sd 24.552

hc_sex.answer: Discovery dataset: F 613 (56.81%), M 466 (43.19%); Validation dataset: F 641 (58.06%), M 463 (41.94%)

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: Discovery dataset: DPARSF v5.4 (Data Processing Assistant for Resting-State fMRI); slice-timing and head-motion correction; normalization to MNI space using EPI template; 3-mm isotropic voxels; 6-mm FWHM Gaussian smoothing; regression of Friston-24 head-motion parameters, white matter and CSF signals; bandpass filtering (0.01-0.1 Hz); scrubbing procedure. Validation dataset: slice-timing and head-motion correction; linear detrending; regression of Friston-24 head-motion parameters, white matter and CSF signals; DARTEL normalization to MNI space; bandpass filtering (0.01-0.1 Hz). Brain parcellation: Brain Connectome Atlas (Fan et al., 2016) with 246 regions

quality_checking_detail.answer: Quality control for both clinical and imaging data was performed. Mean framewise displacement (FD) was calculated and used as a covariate in statistical analyses. A scrubbing procedure was performed in the discovery dataset. FD was controlled for in group-level comparisons and clinical association analyses.

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: ComBat harmonization was independently performed in each dataset to minimize site effects on ALFF values. Site was also included as a covariate in group-level analyses (two-sided two-sample t-tests controlling for age, sex, site, and mean FD). ComBat is capable of removing unwanted site variation while preserving biological variability.

software_tool.answer: GAUSSIAN PROCESS REGRESSION AND CLASSIFICATION Toolbox version 4.2 (http://www.GaussianProcess.org/gpml/code)

response_variable.answer: ALFF (Amplitude of Low-Frequency Fluctuations) for 246 brain regions (Brain Connectome Atlas)

predictor_effects.answer: Age and Sex are modeled as fixed effects in the Gaussian process regression.

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The study explicitly addresses multiple nuisance structures: (1) Site effects were handled through ComBat harmonization independently in each dataset, which removes unwanted site variation while preserving biological variability. (2) Site was included as a covariate in group-level analyses. (3) Head motion (mean FD) was calculated and included as a covariate in statistical analyses. (4) Age and sex were modeled in the normative model as predictors. The study demonstrates awareness of and appropriate handling of key nuisance factors (site, motion, age, sex).

Group-level differences between patients and HCs were derived through a twosided two-sample t test while controlling for age, sex, site, and mean frame-wise displacement (FD) (Han et al., 2018, 2020) for each brain region.

This uses non-independent data from the same domain (same training dataset split into folds). MSE (mean squared error) was calculated between true and predicted ALFF values.

This provides independent validation within the same domain (same dataset but different sites). MSE values were calculated to assess generalizability.

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason:
The study trained the Gaussian process regression model on healthy controls from the discovery dataset (DIDA-MDD) and tested it on healthy controls from the validation dataset (REST-meta-MDD), and vice versa. These two datasets are from different consortia with different acquisition equipment, protocols, and preprocessing strategies, representing different domains. MSE values between predicted and true ALFF values were calculated to demonstrate cross-domain generalizability.

clinical_dataset.answer: Discovery dataset: DIDA-MDD (9 sites); Validation dataset: REST-meta-MDD consortium (25 sites)

clinical_groups_n.answer: Discovery dataset: MDD:1148; Validation dataset: MDD:1276

clinical_groups_age.answer: Discovery dataset: MDD mean 33.83 (SD 14.97); Validation dataset: MDD mean 36.23 (SD 213.78)

clinical_groups_sex.answer: Discovery dataset: MDD F 673 (58.62%) M 475 (41.38%); Validation dataset: MDD F 813 (63.71%) M 463 (36.29%)

deviation_metric.answer: Z-score calculated from normative model; extreme deviation defined as |Z| > 2.6 (corresponding to p < 0.005); individualized ALFF abnormalities decomposed into factor compositions (weights) using non-negative matrix factorization (NMF)

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Group-level comparisons: Two-sided two-sample t-tests between patients and HCs controlling for age, sex, site, and mean FD, with Bonferroni correction for subtype analyses and FDR correction for other analyses. Clinical associations: (1) Episodicity (first-episode vs recurrent): spatial correlations between factors and two-sample t-tests for factor compositions. (2) Medication status (treated vs untreated): spatial correlations and two-sample t-tests. (3) Symptom severity: Pearson's correlations between factor compositions and HAMD total scores, illness duration, age of onset. (4) Sex differences: two-sample t-tests between female and male patients. (5) Motion effects: Pearson's correlations between factor compositions and mean FD. Multilinear regression models were used to link differential factors to: group-level abnormalities (unthresholded t-statistic vectors), neurotransmitter receptor/transporter distributions, and transcriptional profiles of inflammation-related genes. Permutation testing (10,000 permutations) was used to assess significance. Gaussian mixture models (GMM) were used for subtyping based on factor compositions, with BIC for optimal cluster number selection.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Four robust differential factors (2 positive, 2 negative) underlying individual ALFF abnormalities were identified, explaining 57.19% of variance; these factors were associated with clinical features (medication, episodicity, symptom severity), neurotransmitter distributions (explaining up to 78% of variance), inflammation-related gene expression, and structural covariance networks; factor compositions identified four reproducible MDD subtypes with distinct ALFF patterns and clinical characteristics.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: The study identified two positive and two negative differential factors underlying individualized ALFF abnormalities in MDD, which were highly reproducible across discovery and validation datasets (spatial correlations: 0.77, 0.85, 0.67, 0.80 respectively, all FDR-corrected p < 1.00e-4). These factors explained 57.19% (±6.84%) of variance in individualized ALFF abnormalities, significantly more than chance (permutation p < 1.00e-4), and accounted for 71% of group-level ALFF abnormalities in the discovery dataset and 68% in the validation dataset. Clinical associations revealed that: (1) treated patients showed significantly lower weights of positive factors and higher weights of negative factors compared to untreated patients; (2) recurrent patients exhibited significantly lower weights of negative factor 1 than first-episode patients (t=-3.77, Cohen's d=-0.46); (3) HAMD scores were positively correlated with positive factors and negatively with negative factors. Neurobiological correlates showed that neurotransmitter receptor/transporter distributions explained 52-78% of variance in the differential factors (all FDR-corrected p < 1.00e-4), with M1, DAT, and A4B2 playing important roles. Positive factor 2 and negative factor 2 were significantly correlated with transcriptional profiles of inflammation-related genes (R=-29.07e-2 and -37.96e-2 respectively, FDR-corrected p < 1.00e-4). All factors were informed by normal structural covariance networks (correlations: 0.46, 0.22, 0.25, 0.44, all FDR-corrected p < 1.00e-5) and demonstrated distinct epicenters. Factor compositions revealed four stable subtypes with unique ALFF patterns: subtype 1 showed overall decreased ALFF, subtype 2 showed overall increased ALFF, subtype 3 showed increased ALFF in putamen/striatum but decreased in calcarine/lingual/cuneus, and subtype 4 showed modest increases in inferior temporal gyrus, parahippocampus, and frontal regions. Cross-dataset subtyping showed good replicability (ARI: 0.52 and 0.39).
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: First, insufficient clinical information such as symptom dimensions and comorbidities limited exploration of whether differential factors correspond to specific symptom dimensions or are influenced by comorbidities. Second, while medication effects on factor compositions were observed, quantitative analysis of relationships between factor composition changes and specific medication variables (types, doses) was not conducted. Third, only cross-sectional data were included, restricting insights into the evolution of differential factors with disease progression over time.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: The study demonstrates that a dimensional framework using shared differential factors can reconcile the contradiction between substantial individual heterogeneity in neuroimaging abnormalities and phenotypic similarities among MDD patients. The identification of four reproducible subtypes based on factor compositions offers potential for personalized biomarkers for diagnosis and treatment. The framework effectively bridges individual-level abnormalities with group-level findings, enhancing interpretability. The factors' associations with neurotransmitter distributions and gene expression profiles provide links between macroscale neuroimaging abnormalities and microscale biological mechanisms. The network-based epicenter findings align with spreading hypotheses of psychiatric pathology and suggest divergent disease progression pathways.

general_notes.general_notes: This study represents a comprehensive investigation of heterogeneity in spontaneous neural activity abnormalities in MDD using two large multi-center datasets (total 2424 MDD patients and 2183 HCs). The study is notable for its rigorous validation strategy including: (1) replication in an independent dataset with different equipment, protocols, and preprocessing; (2) multiple validation strategies for normative modeling (10-fold CV, leave-one-site-out CV, cross-dataset validation, validation with different brain atlases); (3) extensive sensitivity analyses. The study used non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) to decompose individualized ALFF abnormalities into shared differential factors, a novel approach that provides a dimensional perspective on heterogeneity. Discovery dataset demographics: 1148 MDD patients (age 33.83±14.97, 58.62% female), 1079 HCs (age 33.96±13.87, 56.81% female), 9 sites, HAMD 21.31±6.77, illness duration 2.10±3.60 years, 512 first-episode/79 recurrent, 277 medicated/622 unmedicated. Validation dataset demographics: 1276 MDD patients (age 36.23±213.78, 63.71% female), 1104 HCs (age 36.15±245.52, 58.06% female), 25 sites, HAMD 20.50±58.71, illness duration 3.04±24.74 years, 538 first-episode/282 recurrent, 408 medicated/447 unmedicated. Imaging was acquired using 3.0T GE or Siemens scanners with gradient-echo planar imaging sequences. The study found maximum overlap of regional extreme deviations was only 9% in discovery dataset and 6% in validation dataset, confirming substantial heterogeneity. Non-negative matrix factorization was also validated using different numbers of factors (K=2-10), with generalizability error reaching minimum at K=2 for both positive and negative factors. The framework successfully identified four subtypes that differed significantly in clinical characteristics including HAMD scores and illness duration.
